items.stem: On what date was President Habyarimana’s plane shot down over Kigali?
items.answer: 6 April 1994
items.markingKey: 6 April 1994. The plane, also carrying Burundi’s President Ntaryamira, was hit by missiles on the evening of 6 April.

items.stem: Explain why the speed of the killing in Rwanda suggests prior planning.
items.answer: Within hours roadblocks were set up, lists of targets were used, militias had been armed and trained and the interim government directed officials to mobilise the population – which required preparation.

items.stem: "Only a small group of soldiers carried out the killing." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Hundreds of thousands of civilians were mobilised alongside the army and Interahamwe; gacaca later handled about 1.9 million cases.

items.answer: There was clear central organisation and preparation, but local mobilisation and wartime dynamics shaped how the genocide unfolded.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Chapter VI mandate"?
options: Acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as defined in the UN Genocide Convention of 1948
The US policy of May 1994 that set strict conditions for American support of UN peacekeeping after the Somalia debacle
The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, created by UN Security Council Resolution 955 in November 1994 and based in Arusha, Tanzania
A UN peacekeeping mandate based on the consent of the parties, allowing force only in self-defence
items.answer: A UN peacekeeping mandate based on the consent of the parties, allowing force only in self-defence
items.markingKey: D. "Chapter VI mandate" is a UN peacekeeping mandate based on the consent of the parties, allowing force only in self-defence.

items.stem: A student claims that the UN had no troops in Rwanda when the genocide began. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: UNAMIR had about 2,500 troops in April 1994; the Security Council chose to reduce them rather than reinforce.
items.markingKey: UNAMIR had about 2,500 troops in April 1994; the Security Council chose to reduce them rather than reinforce. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the mandate given to Opération Turquoise and UNAMIR’s mandate.
items.answer: UNAMIR operated under Chapter VI with consent and limited use of force; Turquoise was authorised under Chapter VII to use “all necessary means” for humanitarian objectives for two months.
items.markingKey: UNAMIR operated under Chapter VI with consent and limited use of force; Turquoise was authorised under Chapter VII to use “all necessary means” for humanitarian objectives for two months. items.stem: Briefly explain why the RPF government formed in July 1994 included Hutu politicians.
items.answer: To present itself as a government of national unity based on the Arusha framework and to reassure the majority population and international donors.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: To present itself as a government of national unity based on the Arusha framework and to reassure the majority population and international donors. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source C: Paraphrased testimony of a genocide survivor from Butare, interviewed by a researcher for Penal Reform International, 2007

In the gacaca sessions I heard who killed my family and where their bodies were. Some confessed and asked for forgiveness. I forgave, but it is not easy to live beside them.

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for an historian studying justice and reconciliation in Rwanda after 1994.
items.answer: Value: A first-hand view from a participant during the gacaca process, showing its personal impact. Limitations: One individual’s experience; the purpose of the interview (evaluating gacaca) may shape answers; survivors could feel pressure to express official reconciliation messages.
items.markingKey: Value: A first-hand view from a participant during the gacaca process, showing its personal impact. Limitations: One individual’s experience; the purpose of the interview (evaluating gacaca) may shape answers; survivors could feel pressure to express official reconciliation messages. items.stem: A student claims that only a small group of soldiers carried out the killing. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Hundreds of thousands of civilians were mobilised alongside the army and Interahamwe; gacaca later handled about 1.9 million cases.
items.markingKey: Hundreds of thousands of civilians were mobilised alongside the army and Interahamwe; gacaca later handled about 1.9 million cases. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the withdrawal of Belgian troops from the École Technique Officielle (ETO) in Kigali on 11 April 1994 and explain what it reveals about the consequences of international withdrawal.
items.answer: About 2,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu sheltering with Belgian UN troops were left behind; most were killed at Nyanza hill the same day. The episode shows that the presence of even a small armed force deterred killers and its withdrawal had fatal consequences.
items.markingKey: Context (About 2,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu sheltering with Belgian UN troops were left behind; most were killed at Nyanza hill the same day.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The episode shows that the presence of even a small armed force deterred killers and its withdrawal had fatal consequences. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the consequences of international withdrawal.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the overthrow of Mobutu Sese Seko in May 1997 shows the regional spill-over of the Rwandan genocide.
items.answer: AFDL forces, with Rwandan and Ugandan troops, advanced across Zaire; Kabila took Kinshasa and renamed the country the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The genocide’s aftermath transformed central Africa, toppling a long-standing dictator and triggering continental war.
items.markingKey: Context (AFDL forces, with Rwandan and Ugandan troops, advanced across Zaire; Kabila took Kinshasa and renamed the country the Democratic Republic of the Congo.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The genocide’s aftermath transformed central Africa, toppling a long-standing dictator and triggering continental war. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the regional spill-over of the Rwandan genocide.

items.stem: A student claims that gacaca courts were traditional village courts unchanged since pre-colonial times. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Gacaca was inspired by tradition but was a new state-run system with written laws, categories of crime and the power to impose prison sentences.
items.markingKey: Gacaca was inspired by tradition but was a new state-run system with written laws, categories of crime and the power to impose prison sentences. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased testimony of a survivor from Kibuye prefecture, recorded by African Rights, Rwanda: Death, Despair and Defiance, 1995

They came with lists. The burgomaster told everyone that the Tutsi were the enemy and that anyone who refused to work would be considered an accomplice. By the evening the church was full of bodies.

Source B: Paraphrased from Alison Des Forges, Human Rights Watch, Leave None to Tell the Story: Genocide in Rwanda, 1999

The genocide was not an explosion of ancient hatred. It was a deliberate choice by a modern elite to cultivate hatred and fear in order to stay in power, carried out through the institutions of the state.

Compare and contrast what Sources A and B reveal about the course of the genocide in Rwanda, April–July 1994.
items.answer: Both show that the killing was organised rather than spontaneous. The survivor describes local officials using lists and coercion at one site, while Des Forges generalises that the genocide was a deliberate elite strategy using the state; A is specific and experiential, B national and analytical.
items.markingKey: Both show that the killing was organised rather than spontaneous. The survivor describes local officials using lists and coercion at one site, while Des Forges generalises that the genocide was a deliberate elite strategy using the state; A is specific and experiential, B national and analytical. Award 1 mark per valid, explicitly linked point of comparison or contrast, up to [4]; at least one comparison and one contrast are needed for full marks. A running (integrated) comparison is preferred to end-on description; do not credit points about provenance in this question.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from Roméo Dallaire, UNAMIR commander, Shake Hands with the Devil: The Failure of Humanity in Rwanda, 2003

With 5,000 well-equipped soldiers and a mandate to act, I could have stopped the killing. Instead, the world looked away, and the Security Council debated words while hundreds of thousands died.

Source B: Christine Shelly, US State Department spokesperson, press briefing in Washington, 10 June 1994 (extract)

Q: How would you describe the events taking place in Rwanda? A: Based on the evidence we have seen, we have every reason to believe that acts of genocide have occurred. Q: How many acts of genocide does it take to make genocide? A: That’s just not a question that I’m in a position to answer.

Using the sources and your own knowledge, discuss the view that the failure of the international community to prevent the genocide in Rwanda was due mainly to the policies of the United States.
items.answer: The USA bore great responsibility as the most powerful member, but failure was collective, involving the UN, Belgium and France.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – supporting: US blocked reinforcement and avoided the term genocide; PDD-25 after Somalia; US delayed UNAMIR II equipment. Challenging: Belgian withdrawal and lobbying; French support for the regime; UN Secretariat ignored Dallaire’s warnings; lack of interest from all permanent members. Judgement: The USA bore great responsibility as the most powerful member, but failure was collective, involving the UN, Belgium and France. Candidates must use both sources and their own knowledge; Markbands – 6–8: focused response; effective use of the sources and accurate own knowledge, integrated (synthesised) to support a clear, balanced judgement; 4–5: some focus on the question; uses sources or own knowledge, with some analysis but little synthesis; 1–3: limited understanding; generalised comments, sources or own knowledge used descriptively; 0: does not reach the standard of the descriptors below.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the most important consequence of the Rwandan genocide was its impact on the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
items.answer: The Congo wars were the deadliest consequence, but the genocide also transformed Rwanda and international humanitarian norms.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: refugee crisis and militarised camps; First and Second Congo Wars with millions dead; continuing conflict in the Kivus. Arguments against: domestic transformation of Rwanda under the RPF; development of international justice (ICTR); emergence of the Responsibility to Protect. Supported judgement: The Congo wars were the deadliest consequence, but the genocide also transformed Rwanda and international humanitarian norms. Markbands: Use the IB Paper 2/3 markbands, scaled to the marks: top band – clearly focused, well structured, accurate and relevant knowledge used to support critical analysis, different perspectives evaluated, reasoned conclusion; middle band – mostly accurate knowledge, some analysis but partly narrative; lower band – little understanding of the demands, mainly description.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "interim government"?
options: Rwandan legislation (2008, revised 2013) criminalising expressions that promote or deny genocide, criticised for restricting free speech
Community-based courts (2002 pilot, nationwide 2005–2012) with elected lay judges that tried most genocide cases
The militia (“those who attack together”) formed from the MRND youth wing, a principal instrument of the killing in 1994
The extremist government formed on 8–9 April 1994 under President Théodore Sindikubwabo and Prime Minister Jean Kambanda, which directed the genocide
items.answer: The extremist government formed on 8–9 April 1994 under President Théodore Sindikubwabo and Prime Minister Jean Kambanda, which directed the genocide
items.markingKey: D. "interim government" is the extremist government formed on 8–9 April 1994 under President Théodore Sindikubwabo and Prime Minister Jean Kambanda, which directed the genocide.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Opération Turquoise"?
options: Community-based courts (2002 pilot, nationwide 2005–2012) with elected lay judges that tried most genocide cases
The French-led military intervention authorised by Security Council Resolution 929 in June 1994, which created a “safe humanitarian zone” in south-west Rwanda
The expanded UN force of 5,500 troops authorised by Resolution 918 in May 1994, which arrived only after the genocide had ended
The US policy of May 1994 that set strict conditions for American support of UN peacekeeping after the Somalia debacle
items.answer: The French-led military intervention authorised by Security Council Resolution 929 in June 1994, which created a “safe humanitarian zone” in south-west Rwanda
items.markingKey: B. "Opération Turquoise" is the French-led military intervention authorised by Security Council Resolution 929 in June 1994, which created a “safe humanitarian zone” in south-west Rwanda.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Second Congo War (1998–2003) and the First Congo War (1996–1997).
items.answer: The First Congo War overthrew Mobutu with Rwandan and Ugandan backing; the Second began when Kabila turned against his former allies and drew in many African states, causing millions of deaths.
items.markingKey: The First Congo War overthrew Mobutu with Rwandan and Ugandan backing; the Second began when Kabila turned against his former allies and drew in many African states, causing millions of deaths. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why Belgium withdrew its troops from UNAMIR in April 1994.
items.answer: Ten Belgian paratroopers were murdered on 7 April; facing domestic outrage, the government withdrew its contingent and lobbied for the whole force to be withdrawn.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Ten Belgian paratroopers were murdered on 7 April; facing domestic outrage, the government withdrew its contingent and lobbied for the whole force to be withdrawn. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that the genocide ended all violence in Rwanda in July 1994. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Violence continued: RPF reprisal killings, the Kibeho massacre (April 1995), insurgent attacks from Zaire and wars in Congo.
items.markingKey: Violence continued: RPF reprisal killings, the Kibeho massacre (April 1995), insurgent attacks from Zaire and wars in Congo. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that the ICTR tried everyone who took part in the genocide. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It tried only senior leaders; most perpetrators were tried by Rwandan national courts and gacaca.
items.markingKey: It tried only senior leaders; most perpetrators were tried by Rwandan national courts and gacaca. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the use of sexual violence during the genocide and explain what it reveals about the gendered nature of the genocide.
items.answer: UN estimates suggest that between 250,000 and 500,000 women were raped; the ICTR’s Akayesu judgment (1998) recognised rape as an act of genocide. Sexual violence was used systematically to destroy Tutsi as a group, reflecting propaganda that depicted Tutsi women as enemies.
items.markingKey: Context (UN estimates suggest that between 250,000 and 500,000 women were raped; the ICTR’s Akayesu judgment (1998) recognised rape as an act of genocide.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Sexual violence was used systematically to destroy Tutsi as a group, reflecting propaganda that depicted Tutsi women as enemies. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the gendered nature of the genocide.

What is the message of Source A about the international response to the Rwandan genocide?
items.answer: A modest, well-equipped force with a proper mandate could have stopped the genocide, but the international community failed to act.

items.stem:
Source B: Paraphrased statement attributed to Paul Kagame, Rwandan Vice-President and Minister of Defence, interview with Western journalists, 1996

We will not allow those who committed genocide to use the camps across our border to come back and finish their work. The international community feeds them; we must protect our people.

Assess the usefulness of Source B to an historian investigating the RPF victory and the regional consequences of the genocide, referring to who produced it, when, why and what it contains.
items.answer: Value: It shows the Rwandan government’s justification for intervention in Zaire, given by its most powerful leader. Limitations: It is a public justification that omits Rwanda’s economic interests in eastern Congo and the abuses by Rwandan-backed forces against refugees.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from Human Rights Watch, Justice Compromised: The Legacy of Rwanda’s Community-Based Gacaca Courts, May 2011

Gacaca achieved remarkable speed and engaged communities in confronting the genocide, but trials were marred by limits on the right to defence, intimidation of witnesses and corruption, and it excluded crimes committed by RPF soldiers.

Explain the view of justice and reconciliation in Rwanda after 1994 that is presented in Source A.
items.answer: Gacaca was fast and participatory but compromised by unfair trial procedures and its exclusion of RPF crimes.

“The genocide in Rwanda was planned and directed from the top.” Using Sources A and B and your own knowledge, how far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: There was clear central organisation and preparation, but local mobilisation and wartime dynamics shaped how the genocide unfolded.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – supporting: lists, arms caches and militia training before April 1994 (Dallaire’s fax); interim government orders and removal of resisting officials; RTLM coordination.
